Otherwise, internal PACS/CSIP/HAS client state is corrupted with bogus addresses. The defects are reads only, and the attacker does not control the address that is dereferenced. The fix adds bt_conn_is_type(conn, BT_CONN_TYPE_LE) checks at the top of the affected callbacks.

The Intel SEDI I2C controller driver (drivers/i2c/i2c_sedi.c, used on Intel ISH platforms) waits for each asynchronous transfer with k_sem_take() on a per-controller completion semaphore and a 1 s timeout. When the wait times out, i2c_sedi_api_full_io() aborts the transfer via SEDI_I2C_ABORT_TRANSFER, but if the controller's completion interrupt fires between the timeout expiring and the abort masking interrupts, the callback k_sem_give()s the semaphore and the token is never discarded.

The next transfer on that bus then takes the stale token immediately and returns success (the stale context->err is usually 0) while the controller is still executing it. The HAL interrupt handler (or DMA) keeps copying received bytes into the caller's msgs[i].buf. Since I2C callers typically pass stack buffers, this writes into a stack frame that has already been returned from, and the caller also consumes incomplete data. The desynchronization can persist across later transfers.

Triggering the race requires a transfer to complete just after the 1 s timeout. A device on the I2C bus that controls clock stretching (for example a malicious or tampered peripheral) can steer this timing, and it also supplies the bytes that get written. Exploitation therefore needs physical access to the bus and is timing-dependent. The impact is corruption of kernel or thread stack memory with data the peripheral controls, which can lead to a crash or potentially to code execution. The fix calls k_sem_reset() and clears context->err after the abort, while the transfer mutex is still held.

The mount-time recovery scan of the Zephyr Memory Storage (ZMS) key-value store, zms_recover_last_ate() in subsys/kvss/zms/zms.c (subsys/fs/zms/zms.c in older releases), computes the end of the sector's data area incorrectly. Every valid allocation table entry (ATE) reset the data-end bound to the start of the sector, including entries whose value is stored inline (8 bytes or less) and delete entries. When the newest ATE in the active sector is one of these, the scan continues past the ATE area into the payload area and reads stored value bytes as struct zms_ate records.

Any payload slot that passes the ATE check (a CRC8 plus the one-byte sector cycle count) is adopted as the newest entry. zms_init() then sets fs->ate_wra and fs->data_wra from it. The pointers are only this weak check away from data an application may have stored on behalf of a remote party: a BLE-writable device name, provisioned credentials, or configuration received over the network. An attacker who can get about 16 bytes of chosen content persisted in a ZMS value can plant a forged ATE. The forged entry takes effect after the next mount, provided the newest entry in that sector is small or a delete. Random data can also match by chance, which is how the issue was found.

A forged or accidentally matched ATE overrides the stored entry for any chosen id. Its inline data or its offset/len pointer controls what later reads of that key return. The misplaced write pointers also make later writes place ATEs and payloads over other entries' existing data, silently corrupting persistent configuration such as settings values stored in ZMS. The effects are limited to the active flash sector and to what ZMS returns to its callers. No RAM out-of-bounds access was identified.

The Intel SoC FPGA Agilex5 SoC's static MMU region table in soc/intel/intel_socfpga/agilex5/mmu_regions.c mapped the System Manager peripheral (sysmgr) with MT_P_RW_U_RW. That sets the EL0 access-permission bit in the page-table descriptor, so user mode can read and write the block. The other peripheral windows in the same table, and the same block on the sibling Agilex SoC, are correctly mapped MT_P_RW_U_NA.

On arm64, memory-domain page tables are cloned from the kernel page tables (arch_mem_domain_init()). When CONFIG_USERSPACE is enabled, every user mode thread therefore gets direct load/store access to the System Manager registers, with no partition grant or system call. Any untrusted code running as a user thread can exploit this.

The System Manager controls system-wide state that only the kernel should own: NoC/FPGA-bridge idle requests, SDMMC and EMAC interface configuration, FPGA interface enables and boot scratch registers. A user thread can stall the interconnect or reconfigure peripherals out from under kernel drivers, causing denial of service and integrity loss for the platform, and can read that configuration. This breaks the userspace isolation boundary. Builds without CONFIG_USERSPACE (the default) are not affected. The fix maps the region MT_P_RW_U_NA.

The Zephyr TFTP client in subsys/net/lib/tftp/tftp_client.c does not check where the reply to its request comes from. After sending a read or write request to the configured server, send_request() accepts the first UDP datagram that arrives on the client's socket from any address and port. It then calls zsock_connect() to that sender, so the sender becomes the peer for the rest of the transfer. RFC 1350 requires a client to discard datagrams whose source does not match the transfer ID it expects.

A host that can send a UDP datagram to the client's ephemeral port before the real server replies can take over the transfer. It can reply from its own address and does not need to spoof the server. A host on the same network segment that sees the request can do this easily. An off-path attacker must guess the randomized ephemeral port and win the race, which is easier when the server is slow or unreachable. No authentication or user interaction is needed beyond the device starting a transfer through tftp_get() or tftp_put(), for example from an application or the net tftp shell command.

For tftp_get(), the attacker chooses the entire content handed to the application's data callback. For tftp_put(), the whole upload buffer is sent to the attacker. There is no memory corruption. TFTP itself has no authentication, and after the fix an attacker who can spoof the server's IP address can still interfere with a transfer. The fix checks the server's address on the first reply and the full address and port on every later datagram, and drops mismatches without using up the transfer's retries.

usbh_req_setup() in subsys/usb/host/usbh_ch9.c returns -ETIMEDOUT as soon as a control request times out, even though the transfer is still in flight. usbh_xfer_dequeue() only requests cancellation, and the host controller driver keeps the transfer and its data buffer until it returns it through the completion callback. Callers such as usbh_req_desc_dev() and usbh_req_desc_cfg() free the buffer (net_buf_unref()) right after usbh_req_setup() returns. Separately, a single global semaphore (ch9_req_sync) with no mutual exclusion lets a late or foreign completion wake the wrong waiter. That waiter then returns early and its caller frees a buffer the controller is still filling.

A malicious USB device attached to a Zephyr USB host port can trigger this during enumeration. It NAKs a GET_DESCRIPTOR request until the 5-second timeout expires, then answers with data around the cancellation, or delays its answer to the next request after leaving a stale semaphore signal. The controller driver (for example the MAX3421E max3421e_hrslt_success() path) then writes device-controlled bytes into the freed net_buf and updates its length.

The result is a use-after-free write into the USB host buffer pool with attacker-chosen contents, which can corrupt buffers that have been reallocated to other transfers, plus a leak of transfer objects. Crashes or memory corruption follow. The fix serializes usbh_req_setup() with a mutex, resets the semaphore before each request, and waits for the driver to return a cancelled transfer before freeing it. Only builds with the experimental CONFIG_USB_HOST_STACK are affected.

The STM32 SMBus driver (drivers/smbus/smbus_stm32.c) implements smbus_block_read() and smbus_block_pcall() by issuing a single i2c_transfer() in which the byte-count byte returned by the peripheral is read directly into the len field of the following i2c_msg. That message then receives data straight into the caller-supplied buffer. Nothing bounds the count, so smbus_stm32_block_read() and smbus_stm32_block_pcall() read up to 255 bytes into a buffer that the SMBus API documents (and the syscall verifiers validate) as holding at most SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX (32) bytes.

The count is chosen by the addressed SMBus peripheral. A malicious, counterfeit or faulty device on the bus (for example a removable smart battery, PMBus supply or plug-in module), or anyone able to drive the bus lines, can report a block count above 32 and cause the driver to write up to 223 bytes past the end of the caller's buffer. Callers typically pass a 32-byte stack buffer, as the in-tree smbus block_read shell command does, so the overflow lands on the caller's stack before any caller-side count check can run.

The result is attacker-controlled stack or memory corruption in the context of the calling thread, which can crash the system or potentially be leveraged for code execution. When the call arrives through the smbus_block_read/smbus_block_pcall system calls, the out-of-bounds write happens in supervisor mode beyond the 32-byte region validated for the user thread. The fix receives the block into a driver-local 255-byte buffer and copies it out only when the count is at most SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX, returning -ENODATA otherwise.

The OpenThread PSA crypto platform backend in modules/openthread/platform/crypto_psa.c only supported PSA key references. otPlatCryptoAesSetKey() copied aKey->mKeyRef into the AES context unconditionally. On an OpenThread Radio Co-Processor (RCP) build, CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_CRYPTO_PSA does not select CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_PLATFORM_KEY_REF, so OpenThread passes the MAC key as literal bytes and mKeyRef is uninitialized. psa_cipher_encrypt() in otPlatCryptoAesEncrypt() then fails without writing its output, and the error is only caught by an OpenThread assertion that is compiled to a no-op when CONFIG_ASSERT is disabled.

When the RCP handles transmit security in software, AES-CCM* is never keyed. That is the case with Thread 1.2 or later, where CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_MAC_SOFTWARE_TX_SECURITY_ENABLE defaults to y, on a radio driver without IEEE802154_HW_TX_SEC. Every MAC key-id-mode-1 frame goes out with its payload XORed against a single 16-byte pad of stale stack data, reused for every block, and with an unkeyed MIC. CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_CRYPTO_PSA is enabled by default since v4.4.0.

A passive attacker within 802.15.4 radio range can recover the pad from predictable plaintext (for example 6LoWPAN headers) and read the payload of the frames the device transmits. The practical impact is limited. The configuration is not the default (the default Thread version is 1.1), and the same defect makes peers reject every secured data frame, so an affected device cannot exchange data on the network. Received traffic and key distribution are not affected. With CONFIG_ASSERT enabled, the RCP halts on the first secured transmission instead.

ethernet_send() in subsys/net/l2/ethernet/ethernet.c dropped the caller's reference on an IPv4 packet whenever net_arp_prepare() returned NET_ARP_PKT_REPLACED. That return value is also used when ARP could not queue the packet because every ARP cache entry is already pending. In that case ARP holds no reference of its own, so the original packet was freed before the replacing ARP request was transmitted.

If transmitting the ARP request then failed (a driver send error or an ethernet_fill_header() failure), the error path called net_pkt_ref() on the freed packet. net_if_tx() then called net_pkt_unref() on it again. If the freed net_pkt slab slot was reallocated in between, the stray unref releases a reference owned by an unrelated packet, which is freed while still in use.

An attacker on the local link can drive the ARP cache into the all-pending state. CONFIG_NET_ARP_TABLE_SIZE defaults to 2, so it is enough to elicit replies to a few spoofed, non-responding on-subnet addresses. Reaching the memory corruption also needs a transmit failure the attacker does not directly control and a narrow slab-reuse race. The practical impact is corruption or a crash of the network stack (denial of service).

TeamPass is a self-hosted collaborative password manager. Prior to 3.2.1.2, the update_folder action in app/sources/folders.queries.php allowed an authenticated, non-read-only user to re-parent a folder without checking whether the target folder or submitted parentId belonged to the caller's user-accessible_folders set. Selecting a personal folder as the new parent passed the personal-folder guard and set personal_folder on the target, transferring the credential subtree into the attacker's accessible space after the next login and hiding it from the organization, including administrators. The change exposed credential labels, logins, URLs, email addresses, and descriptions, while sharekey-protected passwords remained protected; hiding the subtree also denied other users access. This issue is fixed in version 3.2.1.2.

A heap-based buffer overflow flaw was found in rpm. RPMTAG_FILESIGNATURES in a crafted, unsigned RPM package's main header is declared with the wrong header type, causing hex2binv() to allocate a one-byte buffer and then write the tag's attacker-controlled, hex-decoded content — of attacker-chosen length — past the end of that allocation. This is reachable via rpm2cpio, rpm2archive, and rpm -qlvp on an untrusted package.

Improper input validation in some SPARQL functions available in Apache Jena ARQ allows users to submit SPARQL queries that cause excessive CPU and/or memory usage.  This may be the result of intentionally malicious inputs in the query itself, or an expression applied over data that has been insufficiently validated/sanitised

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 6.3.0, which fixes this issue.

A flaw was found in SoupServer (libsoup). When an HTTP/1.x client sends a request with Expect: 100-continue and a request body, and SoupServer returns an early final (non-1xx) response before the body is read, the server neither drains the declared body bytes nor closes the connection. On a keep-alive connection, those leftover bytes are interpreted as a subsequent HTTP request. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can place a complete HTTP request in the body and cause SoupServer to process that smuggled request, leading to unintended request handling.

A flaw was found in GEGL. The Radiance HDR loader reads past the end of a memory-mapped image when an uncompressed scanline is shorter than the width declared in the file header. Opening a crafted HDR file crashes the application that uses the loader.

Improper neutralization of input during web page generation ('cross-site scripting') vulnerability in ITG Bilgisayar Teknolojileri Grubu Ltd. Şti. VSRM allows XSS Through HTTP Headers.

This issue affects vSRM: from v14.08.3 before v14.08.5.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains an OS Command Injection vulnerability. A high privileged attacker with local access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to arbitrary command execution.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains a Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop') vulnerability. An unauthenticated attacker with remote access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to a Denial of service.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains a Stack-based Buffer Overflow vulnerability. An unauthenticated attacker with remote access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to a Denial of service.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains a null pointer dereference vulnerability. An unauthenticated remote attacker with adjacent network access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to a denial of service condition.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability. An unauthenticated remote attacker with adjacent network access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to cause denial of service condition.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains an OS Command Injection vulnerability. An unauthenticated adjacent network attacker could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to arbitrary command execution. This vulnerability is considered critical as it may allow unauthenticated command execution.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains a heap based buffer overflow. An unauthenticated remote attacker with adjacent network access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to a denial of service condition.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability. An unauthenticated remote attacker with adjacent network access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to a denial of service condition.

Dell Enterprise Sonic Distribution, versions prior to 4.6.1, contains an Improper Input Validation vulnerability. An unauthenticated attacker with adjacent network access could potentially exploit this vulnerability, leading to a denial of service condition.

The WP Compress – Instant Performance & Speed Optimization plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Directory Traversal in all versions up to, and including, 7.26.00 via the 'css' parameter parameter. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to read the contents of arbitrary files on the server, which can contain sensitive information. Exploiting the file read requires a preparatory unauthenticated request that plants a boundary directory by injecting a path traversal sequence into a cookie listed in WPC_CACHE_COOKIES (such as pll_language, present in the default list), meaning the plugin's cookie-cache feature must be enabled with at least one tracked cookie name configured.

A flaw was found in sssd. This vulnerability allows a local user to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by submitting a specially crafted passkey authentication token that lacks null terminators. The authentication service reads past the end of the provided memory buffer, causing the process to crash and disrupting authentication services.

A flaw was found in SSSD. In configurations where the autofs responder service is enabled, memory allocated during successful request processing is not released until the client connection terminates. A local attacker can exploit this vulnerability by maintaining an open connection and repeatedly submitting valid requests, leading to memory exhaustion and a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in SSSD. An unprivileged local user can repeatedly request master automount map updates through the autofs responder due to missing authorization checks. This triggers global cache invalidation and forces repeated lookups to backend directory providers, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) from degraded automount availability and elevated resource consumption.

A flaw was found in sssd. A remote attacker can cause a denial of service (DoS) by submitting a certificate that lacks an expected Security Identifier (SID) extension. In deployments configured with SID-based certificate mapping rules, the service fails to verify the presence of the extension before processing it, causing the process to crash during authentication or lookup operations.

A flaw was found in SSSD. A local user can cause a denial of service (DoS) by disrupting system authentication services. When handling Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface (GSSAPI) authentication in the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) responder, cached connection state is freed upon completion without clearing the reference pointer. An attacker can exploit this by sending an additional request over the same connection, causing the service to access invalid memory and unexpectedly terminate.

A flaw was found in SSSD. An unprivileged local user can repeatedly request lookups for nonexistent entries through the Name Service Switch (NSS) responder. Because the negative cache does not limit the total number of stored entries and only removes expired records when an existing key is rechecked, the cache can grow without bound. This behavior can lead to memory exhaustion, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) as the responder becomes unresponsive or terminates.

A flaw was found in sssd. A local attacker can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending a crafted Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) request containing a zero-length authentication token to the responder socket. Due to missing input validation, the service attempts to read beyond buffer boundaries when processing the token, causing the PAM responder to crash.

A flaw was found in SSSD. A local attacker with access to the Name Service Switch (NSS) responder UNIX socket can trigger an integer underflow by sending a specially crafted request with an undersized packet header. This issue causes an out-of-bounds memory read during packet parsing, crashing the responder process and resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in sssd. A local attacker can trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending a specially crafted Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) request when passkey authentication is enabled. Due to a missing state validation check in passkey Kerberos handling, the PAM responder dereferences an uninitialized pointer and crashes. This failure disrupts authentication services on the host.

A flaw was found in SSSD. A local user can trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by exploiting a race condition in the autofs responder between asynchronous enumeration completion and map invalidation. By repeatedly sending concurrent map enumeration and invalidation requests, an attacker can cause memory to leak, leading to excessive memory consumption that can disrupt or crash the autofs service.

A flaw was found in SSSD (System Security Services Daemon). When Identity Provider (IdP) authentication is enabled, pre-authentication requests retain state in memory without being cleared or timed out. A local attacker can repeatedly initiate authentication flows without completing them, causing unbounded memory consumption. This memory exhaustion can lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) by degrading or terminating SSSD authentication services.

A flaw was found in SSSD. When configured to use Microsoft Entra ID, search inputs are not properly sanitized before being incorporated into directory query filters. A local user can exploit this vulnerability by submitting a crafted lookup request, manipulating the query logic to cause unauthorized information disclosure from the directory.

A flaw was found in SSSD. In trust-enabled identity management environments, SSSD evaluates Host-Based Access Control (HBAC) rules by stripping domain qualifiers and comparing only short usernames. An authenticated user in a trusted domain who shares the same username as an authorized local account can bypass access policies and gain unauthorized access to protected services or hosts.

LinkAce is a self-hosted archive to collect website links. Prior to 2.6.0, LinkController::update() in app/Http/Controllers/API/LinkController.php passes $request->all() to the repository update method even though user_id is fillable and is not an allowed field in the validated update request. An authenticated API user who is authorized to update a link can therefore assign an arbitrary or nonexistent user_id, transferring the link into another user's bookmark collection or orphaning it from any real account. The web update controller is unaffected because it passes only validated fields. This issue is fixed in version 2.6.0.

aMQTT is an open source MQTT broker and client. From 0.11.0 until 0.11.4, add_subscription() in amqtt/broker.py accepts malformed single-level + wildcard placement because it checks substrings instead of validating each slash-delimited level. The _matches() function converts each + into a greedy regular-expression fragment and evaluates it with re.fullmatch(), allowing a filter containing many adjacent + characters to trigger catastrophic backtracking when compared with a topic that partially matches but ultimately fails. Because matching runs synchronously in _run_broadcast(), one subscription followed by a publish can block the broker event loop, stopping message delivery and new connection processing until restart. Anonymous clients can trigger the issue with the default configuration. Any authenticated client permitted to create arbitrary subscriptions and publish messages may still exploit it when authentication is enabled. This issue is fixed in version 0.11.4.

A flaw was found in libtirpc. The SunRPC UDP/datagram server transport reuses a single receive buffer across requests and resets the XDR decode position without rebinding the decode length to the size of the datagram actually received. As a result, when a short UDP RPC request is received after a longer one, the XDR decoder can read stale bytes left in the reused buffer and interpret them as part of the current request, including credential, verifier, or procedure-argument fields. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to data confidentiality and integrity for services that use a UDP-based SunRPC server.

Improper limitation of a pathname to a restricted directory ('path traversal') vulnerability in Apache BuildStream allows malicious or compromised artifact or execution servers to write files on the host, with the privileges of the user running BuildStream, as part of `bst artifact checkout`.

The impact of this issue is mitigated by:

  *  BuildStream projects should only use trusted servers for remote cache and remote execution as otherwise the build output can also not be trusted


This issue affects Apache BuildStream: through 2.8.1.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.2, which fixes the issue.

A maliciously crafted DWG file, when parsed by Autodesk AutoCAD, can trigger an Integer Overflow vulnerability in RLE bitmap decompression, resulting in an undersized heap allocation and subsequent heap buffer overflow. A malicious actor can leverage this vulnerability to cause a crash or potentially execute arbitrary code in the context of the current process.

OpenRemote is an open-source internet-of-things platform. Prior to 1.31.0, an authenticated user who obtains another user's MQTT session ID can disconnect that session across realm boundaries through the GET route GET {realm}/disconnect/{sessionID}. In manager/src/main/java/org/openremote/manager/security/UserResourceImpl.java, disconnectUserSession ignores the requested realm and calls mqttBrokerService.disconnectSession(sessionID) without checking session ownership; model/src/main/java/org/openremote/model/security/UserResource.java exposes the route without an @RolesAllowed restriction. The earlier cross-realm read-method guards did not cover this disconnect method, and same-realm users can also disconnect sessions they do not own. Session IDs are not trivially brute-forceable but may be exposed through monitoring, logs, or correlated API calls, and the unauthorized disconnect can disrupt MQTT connectivity across tenant boundaries without directly disclosing session data. This issue is fixed in 1.31.0.

The Shortcodes Ultimate plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Local File Inclusion in versions up to, and including, 7.9.1 This is due to su_get_current_url() interpolating the raw Host request header into the authority portion of a URL that is then passed to esc_url() — which by design preserves '[' and ']' inside the authority so IPv6 literal hosts remain valid — and the [su_qrcode] shortcode substituting that value into its data attribute (the documented %CURRENT_URL% token) before feeding it to do_shortcode(). This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to include arbitrary PHP files that reside within the active theme's root directory (bounded because '/' inside an attribute value terminates parse_url()'s host and is then percent-encoded and stripped), and — when the shipped-default 'Unsafe features' option remains on — to read arbitrary post meta of any post, on any front-end page that renders [su_qrcode data="%CURRENT_URL%"].

A flaw was found in GIMP’s X cursor (XMC) thumbnail loader. When GIMP generates a thumbnail for a crafted XMC file, it allocates a pixel buffer using a width * height size computed in 32-bit signed arithmetic. If that product overflows, the allocation is smaller than the true image extent. A subsequent GEGL buffer read uses the unwrapped dimensions and performs an out-of-bounds read on the heap, after integer overflow in the size calculation. This can crash GIMP or corrupt process memory.

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in GIMP’s DICOM export plug-in. When exporting an image with extremely large width and height, the export path allocates a buffer using a 32-bit width * height (and bytes-per-pixel) product that can overflow. GEGL then writes the full uncompressed extent into the undersized buffer, after integer overflow in the allocation size

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in GIMP’s GIF export plug-in. Exporting an image with very large width and height can cause 32-bit overflow when computing the pixel buffer size. The plug-in allocates a buffer based on the wrapped value while GEGL writes using the true image extent, rooted in integer overflow

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in GIMP’s PCX export plug-in. For images with extremely large width and height, buffer allocation uses overflowing 32-bit width * height arithmetic while subsequent GEGL operations use the full extent, after integer overflow in size calculation

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in GIMP’s raw data export plug-in. When exporting very large images, g_malloc() sizing based on overflowing width * height * bytes-per-pixel can allocate far less memory than GEGL reads or writes during export, following integer overflow

A heap-based buffer overflow was found in GIMP’s Hot color filter plug-in. For very large images, a pixel buffer is allocated using overflowing 32-bit width * height (and related) arithmetic while the filter’s pixel access path uses the true image size, after integer overflow in the allocation size

A heap-based buffer overflow flaw was found in Cyrus SASL. The add_to_challenge() function in the DIGEST-MD5 plugin computes the size of the buffer needed for a challenge/response field before DIGEST-MD5 quoting is applied, but does not recompute that size when quoting (escaping special characters) makes the value longer. The under-sized buffer is then passed to strcat(), causing a heap-based out-of-bounds write whose size depends on attacker-controlled input. A malicious or on-path DIGEST-MD5 (or HTTP Digest) server can trigger this flaw in a connecting client by supplying a crafted challenge field, such as realm or nonce, most likely resulting in a crash of the client application.

A flaw was found in m17n-lib. A user providing specially crafted text input can trigger a heap use-after-free condition during input-method state transitions. Under specific conditions, the library frees an internal input context object but subsequently attempts to write to that freed memory. This issue can cause applications relying on the library to crash, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS), or potentially allow arbitrary code execution.

A flaw was found in m17n-lib. By providing crafted input containing an invalid UTF-8 character sequence, an attacker can cause the text parsing function to enter an infinite loop. This issue leads to sustained high CPU utilization, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) for the affected application.

A flaw was found in m17n-lib. An attacker could provide specially crafted or truncated UTF-8 input to trigger an unhandled null pointer dereference during text processing. This issue causes the application to crash unexpectedly, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in flatpak-builder. This vulnerability allows an attacker to cause information disclosure by convincing a user or continuous integration (CI) system to process a crafted build manifest. By specifying local file Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) within source download definitions, the builder bypasses directory confinement checks. As a result, sensitive host files accessible to the build process can be read and incorporated into the build artifacts.

Issue summary: The QUIC stack queues a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame also for
retransmitted NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames. This allows a remote malicious
QUIC stack to queue an unlimited number of RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames.

Impact summary: A malicious remote QUIC peer can trigger an out-of-memory
condition causing a Denial of Service.

CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

Description: The earlier fix for CVE-2026-84784 was not complete. It
failed to ignore retransmissions of the NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame. The QUIC
implementation created and inserted a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame for every
retransmitted NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame it received and there was no limit
on how many RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames were queued.

This issue allows a malicious remote QUIC stack to trigger an unbounded
allocation of memory and eventually an out-of-memory (OOM) condition.

FIPS impact: no
The FIPS module is not affected as the QUIC implementation is outside the
OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

A flaw was found in luksmeta. A local attacker with administrative privileges can cause data corruption when saving metadata to a Linux Unified Key Setup (LUKS) device. Due to incorrect boundary calculations and flawed overlap detection, new metadata entries can be written beyond available free space or over existing records. This issue can corrupt stored encrypted payload data or existing metadata, potentially rendering the affected data inaccessible.

The Unbounce Landing Pages plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting in versions up to, and including, 1.1.6. This is due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping on the proxy error message that is persisted to the 'ub-proxy-error-message' option: unauthenticated attacker-controlled REQUEST_URI data is concatenated into the error string in UBHTTP::stream_request_curl()/stream_request_wp_remote() and stored via update_option(), then later echoed inside a <textarea> on the Unbounce Pages Diagnostics admin page without any escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user (an administrator viewing the Diagnostics screen) accesses an injected page.

A flaw was found in Eye of GNOME (eog). A heap-based buffer overflow exists in the PNG metadata reader due to improper state handling when parsing split metadata chunks. A remote attacker could exploit this flaw by enticing a user into opening a specially crafted PNG file, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution or a Denial of Service (DoS) via application crash.

A flaw was found in CUPS. When processing embedded job ticket comments within documents, the service improperly handles specific IPP attributes, causing an unhandled null pointer dereference. An unauthenticated attacker permitted to submit jobs to a shared printer queue can send a crafted Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) request to crash the print daemon, resulting in a temporary Denial of Service (DoS) for all printing services.

The Flutterwave Payments plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'form_id' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.0.7 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The storing endpoint is accessible without authentication because the required nonce is publicly exposed on any front-end page rendering the plugin's [flw-pay-form], [flw-pay-button], or [flw-donation-form] shortcodes, allowing any unauthenticated visitor to scrape and reuse it.

On Windows, the tarfile "tar" and "data" extraction filters did not reject member names or link targets that have a drive but no root, such as "C:foo". When extracting to a relative destination, such a member was written to the current working directory of that drive instead of the destination, and a symbolic link with such a target pointed outside the destination. The filters now refuse these member names and link targets with AbsolutePathError and AbsoluteLinkError.

A flaw was found in NetworkManager. This local privilege escalation vulnerability exists in NetworkManager's dhclient backend when processing malformed Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) URLs. A local user can exploit this flaw to escalate privileges by triggering a script via a crafted MUD URL, provided an administrator has explicitly configured NetworkManager to use dhclient. This issue does not affect default configurations of NetworkManager.

A flaw was found in libhangul. When parsing Hanja dictionary files, the library fails to verify that an entry contains a valid value alongside its key. By providing a specially crafted dictionary file to an application that queries it, an attacker can trigger an unexpected application crash, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in GIMP. The XCF loader processes image-simulation-intent and image-simulation-bpc parasites without ensuring the parasite data is present before dereferencing it. Opening a specially crafted XCF file with a zero-size simulation parasite can cause a NULL pointer dereference and crash the GIMP application.

The FV Player 8 plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'data.videos[].fv_wp_flowplayer_field_splash' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 8.1.9 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The wp_ajax_fv_player_db_save handler's ownership and capability check is conditional on the presence of the data.update field; omitting it bypasses authorization entirely, allowing a Subscriber-level attacker to overwrite any existing video record using an enumerable video ID — and the valid nonce required by the endpoint is issued to every logged-in visitor of any page hosting the publicly accessible [fvplayer_editor] shortcode.

PHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).

PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE).

A flaw was found in Quay where the robot account listing function constructs a SQL LIKE pattern from user-controlled namespace names without escaping wildcard metacharacters. An attacker who creates a namespace containing an underscore character can match and retrieve robot accounts and their decrypted authentication tokens from other tenants' namespaces, leading to cross-tenant credential theft and unauthorized image operations.

A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.





Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

UNIX symbolic link (symlink) following vulnerability in Apache BuildStream allows source plugins to inadvertently read or write files on the host, with the privileges of the user running BuildStream, via symlinks from malicious or compromised source archives or respositories, as part of source fetching.

The impact of this issue is mitigated by:

  *  BuildStream projects should only use trusted sources in their elements as otherwise the build output can also not be trusted
  *  None of the source plugins in the buildstream, buildstream-plugins or buildstream-plugins-community repositories use the vulnerable `open_file` method


This issue affects Apache BuildStream: through 2.8.1.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.2, which fixes the issue.

lwIP 2.2.0 through 2.2.1, fixed in commit ab2f69c, contains a stack out-of-bounds write vulnerability in mdns_handle_response that allows adjacent attackers to corrupt stack memory by sending mDNS responses with invalid domain names. Attackers on the local link can send multicast PTR answers with oversized RDLENGTH or SRV answers with RDLENGTH below 6 during a service search, overflowing a 256-byte stack buffer and crashing the device.

A flaw was found in Ghostscript as shipped with Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8. Processing a specially crafted PostScript file may allow an attacker to bypass -dSAFER restrictions and access files outside the permitted paths or execute commands with the permissions of the Ghostscript process.

The Python virtual environment (PVE) management endpoints of a computing unit are not authenticated by the application itself. In the local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments, which place no authenticating gateway in front of the services, these endpoints are reachable without credentials. The Kubernetes deployment gates them at the gateway, so only the Kubernetes deployment provides the full security model described in SECURITY.md.



This issue affects Apache Texera (incubating): from 1.1.0 through 1.2.0.



Users are recommended to use the Kubernetes deployment, which enforces the full security model, and to upgrade to 1.3.0-incubating, which documents that the local JVM and single-node Docker Compose deployments do not provide the full security model and should only be used by trusted users.

A flaw was found in cockpit-machines. Red Hat Subscription Management (RHSM) authentication tokens are passed as command-line arguments to background helper processes during image retrieval operations. A local, unprivileged attacker on a system permitting cross-user process inspection can view these arguments while the process is active. This flaw can lead to information disclosure, potentially allowing unauthorized access to RHSM resources within the token's validity period.

A flaw was found in cockpit-machines. When saving Virtual Network Computing (VNC) console settings, the configured password is passed directly as a command-line argument to an underlying system utility. A local unprivileged attacker on a host that allows cross-user process inspection could read the exposed password from the process list while another user modifies settings. This credential disclosure can allow unauthorized access to the guest virtual machine's graphical console.

The system certificate authority (CA) store in Red Hat products, distributed via ca-certificates RPM packages, included multiple root CA certificates of authorities, which signed intermediate CA certificates with weak private keys issued by the eMudhra certificate authority. A man-in-the-middle attacker could use this flaw to issue certificates for arbitrary host names signed by the weak intermediate CA certificates, which would be considered trusted by a TLS/SSL client using system CA store and cause such clients to connect to malicious sites.

Due to inability to only distrust specific intermediate certificates in all clients using the system CA store, root CA certificates of authorities that signed weak intermediate CA certificates are being removed.

codebase-memory-mcp provides local code intelligence for developers and AI agents through a persistent graph and MCP tools. Prior to 0.9.1-rc.1, the optional graph UI's POST /api/process-kill route omitted the indexing-job ownership check on Windows while retaining that check on POSIX systems. A requester able to reach the optional UI could supply an arbitrary process identifier, causing TerminateProcess to stop any process that the server user was permitted to terminate. The flaw affects the Windows-specific process termination path and can cause a high availability impact without disclosing or modifying data. This issue is fixed in version 0.9.1-rc.1.

codebase-memory-mcp provides local code intelligence for developers and AI agents through a persistent graph and MCP tools. Prior to 0.10.0, the indexer's .gitignore matcher implemented * and ** through recursive backtracking without a work bound. A repository containing a pattern with repeated wildcard groups and a long path could make matching work grow exponentially, allowing a single ignore rule to stall discovery indefinitely and, before worker isolation, stall the server. The impact is limited to availability, and the bounded matcher does not claim that every expensive input is eliminated. This issue is fixed in version 0.10.0.

A flaw was found in GCC. An out-of-bounds memory access vulnerability exists in the libstdc++ parallel search implementation due to an undersized internal buffer. A local attacker can exploit this flaw by providing crafted search data to an application compiled with parallel mode, causing the process to crash and leading to a Denial of Service (DoS).

A flaw was found in the libstdc++ component of GCC. An attacker who can provide an excessively large element count to a boolean vector (std::vector<bool>) constructor can trigger an integer wrap during internal memory calculations. This issue leaves the container in an inconsistent state, leading to out-of-bounds memory access and resulting in an application crash or a Denial of Service (DoS) during subsequent operations.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Mobile Field Service product of Oracle E-Business Suite (component: Admin UI).  Supported versions that are affected are 12.2.3-12.2.15. Easily exploitable vulnerability allows low privileged attacker with logon to the infrastructure where Oracle Mobile Field Service executes to compromise Oracle Mobile Field Service.  While the vulnerability is in Oracle Mobile Field Service, attacks may significantly impact additional products (scope change).  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle Mobile Field Service accessible data as well as  unauthorized update, insert or delete access to some of Oracle Mobile Field Service accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 7.3 (Confidentiality and Integrity impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N).

Supported versions that are affected are Oracle Java SE: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3; Oracle GraalVM for JDK: 17.0.21.0.3 and  21.0.13.0.3; Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. A flaw was found in GNU patch. An attacker can achieve arbitrary file creation outside the intended working directory by enticing a user or automated workflow to apply a specially crafted patch file. Due to missing validation during automatic patch reversal, absolute file paths in patch headers are accepted rather than rejected. Consequently, the utility can create files in arbitrary locations with the permissions of the executing user.

A flaw was found in FreeIPA. An improper authorization check allows an authenticated host to retrieve and revoke digital certificates assigned to other users or services. This issue occurs because FreeIPA verifies ownership solely by matching the host name to the certificate's subject Common Name (CN), without confirming actual ownership in the directory service. Consequently, an enrolled host can disrupt services by revoking certificates belonging to other entities.

The out-of-bounds byte is the string's NUL terminator, written at `buffer[buffer_len]`.



Resolution:



Resolution



The bugfix is released with iceoryx2 version 0.10.1 and on main branch (commit 7ca14dd).



Please note that the language bindings for C/C++ and Python (including the iceoryx2-ffi-c crate) are not published to crates.io since they are a local development dependency.

A flaw was found in GCC libstdc++. When an application extracts data into a bitset from a wide-character stream, internal stack memory allocation fails to properly account for character size and alignment. An attacker capable of supplying crafted input to an affected application could trigger a stack-based buffer overflow leading denial of service (DoS).

A flaw was found in the iscsiuio component of open-iscsi. The DHCPv4 option parser incorrectly calculates the length of the options data, causing it to read beyond the allocated buffer into adjacent heap memory. An attacker on the same network segment can send a crafted DHCP response to crash the daemon or corrupt its network configuration.

A flaw was found in the iscsiuio component of open-iscsi. The DHCPv6 option parser calls strlen() on raw network data without ensuring a NUL terminator is present, causing it to read past the buffer into heap memory. This can result in a daemon crash, a 1-byte heap overwrite, or corruption of the iSCSI initiator name. An attacker on the same network segment can trigger this by sending a crafted DHCPv6 Advertise message.

A flaw was found in the iscsiuio component of open-iscsi. The IPv6 Neighbor Discovery handler accesses link-layer address options at a fixed offset without verifying the packet contains them. Additionally, the ARP table is updated unconditionally with attacker-controlled addresses from the packet headers. An attacker on the same network segment can send a minimal Neighbor Advertisement to poison the ARP table and redirect network traffic.

virtualenv is a tool for creating isolated virtual python environments. From 21.14.9 until 21.14.13, the bash bin/activate script can copy an attacker-controlled --prompt value into PS1 without escaping dollar signs or backticks when both promptvars and POSIX mode are disabled during activation. Re-enabling promptvars, running set -o posix, or starting an interactive child bash that inherits the exported PS1 can then expand command substitution in the stored VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT value and execute commands as the user who activates the environment. This issue is fixed in version 21.14.13.

A flaw was found in ansible-core. When a task or its parameters are marked no_log: true, sensitive values passed to a module's warn() or deprecate() calls are not redacted and are printed in cleartext to stdout/stderr in warning and deprecation messages. The 'warnings' and 'deprecations' keys are retained in the PRESERVE allow-list in lib/ansible/_internal/_task.py when the task result is censored, so sensitive parameters bypass masking and can be disclosed in output captured in terminal sessions, CI logs, and any automation wrapping ansible-playbook, even though every task touching the secrets is marked no_log: true.

A remote attacker must authenticate with Read Only (GroupRead) access to at least one Worker Group and reach the Leader API. A crafted expression can exploit the nested compiler to bypass expression restrictions and execute code with the Leader service account's permissions.

An attacker must control pagination data returned by an upstream API or service queried by an existing REST Collector. The Collector must use affected response-based pagination and process the crafted data during a job run. Successful exploitation executes code with the Worker service account's permissions.

An attacker must possess a valid Worker distribution credential, reach the Leader distribution listener, and send crafted authenticated Worker heartbeats. Where mTLS client authentication is enforced, an accepted client certificate and its private key are also required. Successful exploitation bypasses Leader REST authentication and permits administrative API access.

Exploitation requires an identity admitted to a configured trusted IdP application, control of claims selected as the OIDC user identifier, acceptance by configured SSO filters, and a victim with an active Cribl session following a crafted authentication link. Script executes in the Cribl origin, disclosing the victim's session token and permitting access with the victim's privileges; administrator access requires an administrator victim.

An authenticated attacker must reach the Edge file APIs through the Leader or directly on an Edge node. On affected managed Edge deployments with RBAC, Read Only access permits these calls. Disclosure is limited to files readable by the Edge process under its operating-system permissions and capabilities.

NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in Apache Perl.



This issue affects Apache Perl: from 1.99_04 through 2.0.13.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.0.14, which fixes the issue.

Fixed-size stack buffer overflow vulnerability in Apache Perl.



This issue affects Apache Perl: from 1.99_01 through 2.0.13.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.0.14, which fixes the issue.

Stack buffer overflow vulnerability in Apache Perl.



This issue affects Apache Perl: from 1.99_01 through 2.0.13.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.0.14, which fixes the issue.

NULL pointer dereference, Out-of-bounds read vulnerability in Apache Perl.



This issue affects Apache Perl: from 1.99_01 through 2.0.13.



Also fixes an out-of-bounds read in per-request $/ save/restore for which CVE-2026-116021 (now rejected) had previously been assigned.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.0.14, which fixes the issue.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. The Content Synchronization persistent search plugin allows unbounded memory growth when an authenticated client stops reading sync responses, enabling denial of service. Additional race conditions in plugin thread lifecycle can cause crashes during connection teardown or shutdown.

A NULL pointer dereference vulnerability was found in gssproxy. When a GSSX_INIT_SEC_CONTEXT request is received with the target_name field absent, the daemon dereferences the resulting NULL pointer and crashes. The request requires no authentication, allowing any local user to crash the gssproxy daemon via its Unix socket. The daemon does not automatically restart, resulting in a persistent denial of service that also affects dependent services such as Kerberized NFS and IdM.

OOB read vulnerability in Apache Perl.



This issue affects Apache Perl: from 1.99_07 through 2.0.13.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.0.14, which fixes the issue.

OOB read vulnerability in Apache Perl.



This issue affects Apache Perl: from 1.99_01 through 2.0.13.



Note: The over-read data can be returned to the client in the response.



Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.0.14, which fixes the issue.

A NULL pointer dereference flaw was found in 389-ds-base. This flaw occurs when a ModifyDN (rename) operation uses an attribute's schema alias name (such as "commonName") instead of its canonical name (such as "cn") as the new relative distinguished name. An authenticated attacker with the ModifyDN (rename) permission on the affected entry can use this flaw to crash the directory server, causing a denial of service.

Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password vulnerability in ITG Bilgisayar Teknoloji Grubu Tic. Ltd. Şti. VSRM allows Password Recovery Exploitation.

This issue affects vSRM: from v14.08.3 before v14.08.5.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. A type confusion in the SSO token extended operation handler causes partial stack address information to be disclosed in LDAP responses to authenticated users.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. The ldap_utf8prev() function reads bytes before the start of a buffer without bounds checking, causing a heap buffer over-read in string filter parsing that may influence internal filter processing behavior.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. The SMD5 password storage plugin performs unsigned integer underflow when computing salt length from a crafted password hash shorter than 16 bytes, causing a buffer over-read that crashes the LDAP server during authentication.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. The PBKDF2-SHA256 password storage plugin does not enforce an upper bound on the iteration count extracted from stored password hashes. A privileged attacker who can modify a user's password hash can cause excessive CPU consumption during authentication, resulting in denial of service.
Use-after-free in the Layout: Text and Fonts component. This vulnerability was fixed in Firefox 159, Firefox ESR 153.6, Thunderbird 159, Thunderbird 153.6, and Firefox ESR 115.46.

A flaw was found in 389 Directory Server. During schema reload, the attr_syntax_swap_ht() function unconditionally frees attribute syntax information nodes, bypassing the refcount-based deferred deletion used elsewhere in the attribute syntax subsystem. If an administrator triggers schema reload while concurrent LDAP query traffic is active, worker threads may access freed memory, resulting in use-after-free or double-free and a denial of service (server crash).

Module: plugins/modules/keyring_info.py 

CVSS 3.1: 5.5 MEDIUM — AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N 

Issue: The module retrieves a passphrase from the OS native keyring (GNOME Keyring, macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager) and places it directly into result["passphrase"] with no output suppression, no no_log protection, and no documentation warning. 

Root Cause:

Line 105 (protected): keyring_password=dict(type="str", required=True, no_log=True)
Line 127 (NOT protected): result["passphrase"] = passphrase

Observed Output:

{
"changed": false,
"passphrase": "MyMasterP@ssw0rd!SSH_Key_Secret"
}
Visible via register + debug:
{
"keyring_result": {
"changed": false,
"passphrase": "MyMasterP@ssw0rd!SSH_Key_Secret"
}
}

Impact: 

Master passwords, SSH key passphrases and service credentials appear in all Ansible output 

register: keyring_result followed by debug: var=keyring_result prints passphrase in full 

Ansible fact caching backends (Redis, JSON file, memcached) may persist the passphrase 

AWX/Tower job logs silently store the live credential

Fix:

module.exit_json(changed=False, passphrase=passphrase, _ansible_no_log=True)

Also add a documentation warning requiring callers to use no_log: true at the task level.
